    <Input id="email" type="email" aria-invalid={!!errors.email}
           aria-describedby="email-description" />
  </FormGroup>

  <FormGroup label="Name" error="Name is required" htmlFor="name">
    <Input id="name" aria-invalid={!!errors.name}
           aria-describedby="name-description" />
  </FormGroup>

Accessibility contract (aria-describedby wiring):
  FormGroup generates a description element with the ID `{htmlFor}-description`.
  This element holds the hint text, error message, or success confirmation.
  Consumers MUST wire `aria-describedby="{htmlFor}-description"` on their
  input element so that screen readers associate the description with the field.

  The generated ID follows the pattern: `{htmlFor}-description`
  For example, if htmlFor="email", the description ID is "email-description".

  The description element always exists in the DOM (not conditionally rendered)
  so the aria-describedby reference is always valid. Its content changes
  between hint, error, and success states. The container has aria-live="polite"
  so screen readers announce state transitions without interrupting the user.

  The generated hintId is exposed as a read-only derived value via the
  `descriptionId` export on FormGroupProps for consumers who need
  programmatic access rather than hard-coding the ID pattern.

Validation pattern:
  FormGroup manages the error/success display (text, icons, transitions).
  The input atom manages its own border colour via aria-invalid and data-valid
  attributes. Connect them using aria-describedby on the input pointing to
  the FormGroup's generated description ID ({htmlFor}-description).

designDecisions.question: Tailwind v4's default @theme declares --font-mono and --radius, the names Alfons used for its mono face and its base corner radius, so which value a consumer gets depends on stylesheet order. What does Alfons do about the collision?
designDecisions.resolution: Alfons renames both onto names Tailwind's default theme does not declare: --font-monospace for the GT America Mono stack and --radius-base for the base machined corner (var(--radius-2)), with the same values. --font-mono and --radius are retired onto them with lifecycle rows, Alfons's own components, stories, dev surface and prototypes move in the same change (AL-035), and the website moves under AT-095 by following the retired-token rule. From now on an Alfons token never takes a name Tailwind v4's default theme declares: the manifest's tailwindShadowed list, read from the installed tailwindcss/theme.css, is the check, and the tailwind-shadow rule reports any read of such a name.
designDecisions.rationale: The collision is silent: a var() that resolves to Tailwind's value raises nothing, which is how the brand mono face was replaced on four Atlas surfaces before anyone saw it (D-171). On 2026-10-30 the tailwind-shadow rule found 83 reads in Alfons (--font-mono 57, --radius 26) and 87 in the website, and AL-034's three new --font-mono reads made the pre-push ratchet refuse Alfons main at 84e0a94. Simon chose to fix the names rather than accept the rise, because accepting it leaves every new mono or radius read a finding and the class never ends. --font-monospace names the property every reader relies on: the face sets metrics, ids, kickers, captions and code, so --font-code, the name first suggested, would describe a minority of its uses. --radius-base is read by controls and by surfaces such as Tooltip, Modal, Toast and Alert, so a role name such as --radius-control would be wrong for half its readers; re-sorting those reads by role is a separate question. Checked against tailwindcss 4.2.2 node_modules/tailwindcss/theme.css, which declares --font-sans, --font-serif, --font-mono, --font-weight-*, --radius-xs to --radius-4xl and --radius, and neither new name.

designDecisions.question: D-245 settles typography (website wins) and colour, surfaces, elevation and motion (Alfons wins) for absorbing the website's Meccano layer, but not spacing and layout. The website's compat.css remaps --space-5..10 onto smaller rungs (24/32/48/64/96/128px to 20/24/32/40/48/64px), sets its own card padding, page gutters, header height, content width and --radius-message, and reads its own --sp-* ladder directly. Whose spacing and layout values win?
designDecisions.resolution: Alfons's values win for spacing and layout: --space-N, --card-padding and --card-padding-sm, --page-padding-x and its mobile form, --page-top-padding and its mobile form, --header-height, --page-content-max-width and --radius-message keep the values Alfons had before AL-033. Alfons also defines the website's Meccano ladder, --sp-05 to --sp-32 (2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 96 and 128px), as live tokens with the website's values, so the website's direct reads of it keep rendering the same. Consequence: when the website deletes its local layer (AT-076), its pages re-space to Alfons's wider scale wherever they read --space-N or the layout roles.
designDecisions.rationale: Chosen by Simon on 2026-10-29 ("Alfons wins (B)"), extending D-245. Alfons components and Atlas are laid out on Alfons's scale, and Grid's gap prop indexes --space-N as a typed public API, so re-valuing the scale would re-space every consumer to fit one. Keeping the --sp-* ladder live costs nothing and keeps the website's roughly 230 direct reads exact; only the website's remapping of the shared --space-N names gives way.

designDecisions.question: The website loads Alfons and then its own local Meccano layer (src/lib/styles/meccano/), which re-declares 160 Alfons tokens, 63 of them with different values, and adds 51 of its own. When Alfons absorbs that layer so the website can delete it (AL-033, AT-076), whose value wins where the two disagree?
designDecisions.resolution: The website's current value wins for typography and fonts: the families (--font-*, including the Redaction faces), the size ladder and its roles (--fs-*, --text-body, --text-lead), weights (--fw-*), leading (--lh-*), tracking and the --type-* composites. Alfons's value wins for colour, surfaces, elevation and motion, including the AL-025 derived ink steps. Website-only tokens come into Alfons in the layer D-238 requires, or are retired with a lifecycle row whose replacement renders identically. Under D-181's reclassification clause, the retired tokens the website still reads (--type-body, --type-small, --led-off, --shade-part) are reclassified live. Alfons serves every face the website uses as woff2, adding Redaction with its OFL licence. Consequence: Alfons headings and display type move from Moderat to Redaction 35, and --text-body drops from 18px to 15px, in every Alfons consumer.
designDecisions.rationale: Chosen by Simon on 2026-10-29 for the website restyle. The website is the publishing surface, and its typography (the Redaction serif, the 15px body) is the look he wants to publish. Alfons's colour, surface, elevation and motion values are the D-238 theme work of AL-025 to AL-027, made deliberately and more recently than the website's copies, which predate it. Splitting by subject keeps each half's most recent deliberate work, and the comparison script (scripts/compare-website-layer.ts) lists every difference against this rule so the website task can expect each visual change.

designDecisions.question: Alfons has one colour mode, Meccano dark, pinned with data-colour-mode="dark" on <html>, and models admin as a ThemeVariant read through Svelte context: nine Alfons components call getThemeVariant and branch on it, and the website sets it with createThemeContext. D-195 records dark as the sole colour mode. Should Alfons support several themes, and how is a theme applied, so that themes, tokens, components and motion can be swapped independently?
designDecisions.resolution: Alfons supports several themes. A theme is a set of values for the semantic tokens plus a motion preset, applied with a data-theme attribute on any element and inherited by everything inside it through the CSS cascade. Meccano is the default theme and sits on :root. Five rules ride with it. (1) Primitive tokens (the ground, the ink, the steel ramp and the eight part colours) live in files separate from semantic tokens, and a theme file sets semantic tokens only. (2) Components read semantic or component tokens, never primitive tokens, and never branch on a theme in script; the ThemeVariant context and getThemeVariant are retired. (3) Admin becomes an overlay theme, data-theme="admin", which overrides a subset of semantic tokens and inherits the rest. (4) A complete theme sets every semantic token, and an overlay theme sets only semantic tokens; a build check enforces both. (5) data-theme replaces data-colour-mode. This decision makes a light theme possible but does not commit to one. D-195's dark-only constraint on the resolved palette holds until a second complete theme ships; from then the palette is emitted per theme.
designDecisions.rationale: Custom properties inherit, so a theme expressed as token values needs no JavaScript and can restyle one section of a page as easily as the whole page. A theme expressed as a component prop has to be edited into every component for every new theme, which is the opposite of swappable, and it is why admin today needs nine components to branch. Separating primitives from semantics is what lets a theme change roles without touching the raw palette, and the colour derivation in oklab already means most of a new theme is a few base values. Putting motion inside the theme keeps Meccano's machined, no-spring motion a brand choice rather than a global law, so another theme can move differently. Rejected: keeping the ThemeVariant context and adding variants to it (each theme costs an edit per component); a motion layer above all themes (it would force one motion language on every theme); and committing to a light theme now (nothing needs one yet, and D-181 retires what nothing reads).

designDecisions.question: How should Alfons keep its design knowledge current when components are created or design decisions are explicitly confirmed?
designDecisions.resolution: Use deterministic project hooks as event detectors and one idempotent refresh command as the implementation. A component-file write refreshes the derived manifest and synchronises the component vocabulary. A successful ledger record_decision call registers that confirmed decision in Alfons's authored design-memory index and refreshes the manifest. Hooks may record observable facts and confirmed decisions, but must never infer design truth from repetition. The runtime MCP remains read-only over the generated manifest and does not connect to Postgres.
designDecisions.rationale: Alfons already serves a generated manifest, but without an automatic refresh loop its self-description can lag behind the work that created it. Keeping hook logic thin makes the behaviour testable outside an agent session, while retaining Postgres as a build-time authoring dependency preserves D-162's deterministic runtime boundary. Requiring a successful ledger result before indexing a decision prevents drafts, failed calls, and accidental repetition from becoming design law.

designDecisions.question: The Meccano retune left Alfons at 386 tokens against the handoff's 109, with 180 of them pure aliases and 76 referenced by nothing anywhere. What comes out, and on what rule?
designDecisions.resolution: One rule, applied without exception: a token survives only if something reads it, or if something that is read derives from it. Everything else is retired and deleted, with a lifecycle row so the manifest answers with a tombstone rather than silence. Three consequences follow. The duplicate vocabularies go — the eleven --hex-* names, the ten pre-retune brand names, the three American --color-* spellings D-167 has been waiting on since 2026-08-02, and the short --info/--success/--warning/--danger names added during the retune, which lost to the Australian --colour-* spelling that is the house convention and the one consumers already read. The abandoned scales go — --opacity-*, --stroke-*, the four per-edge --card-border-* aliases, the dead half of the widget family, and the surface-tier aliases nothing composed. And the consumer migration is driven from alfons.lifecycle.replacement_name rather than a hand-written map, because that column exists precisely so the migration path is stated once. A deprecated token that turns out to be consumed is reclassified live rather than deleted; deprecation is a judgement about adoption, and adoption is a fact that can change back.
designDecisions.rationale: The 386 was not carelessness, it was accumulation with no counter-pressure: every release added names and none could safely remove them, because before AL-009 there was no way to delete a token without destroying the reason it existed. The tombstone mechanism removed that constraint and nothing had yet spent it. Meccano is what makes the number arguable rather than merely large — it expresses the same visual language, on the same eight hues and the same ground, in 109 tokens, so 386 is not the cost of this design, it is the cost of three vocabularies for it. The alias count is the sharper measure: 180 of 386 definitions are one name pointing at another, which means a reader tracing --hex-red to a value passes through two indirections to reach a hex they could have read directly, and an agent calling get_tokens receives three plausible names for poppy vermilion with nothing to choose between them. That is the exact failure D-165 named for the public chart tokens — an unadopted parallel vocabulary is worse than a speculative one, because both look correct. The retune itself added to the problem and the audit is what surfaced it: --type-prose, --font-sans, --shade-part and the short semantic names were all authored in the last two days against components that do not exist yet, which is the same speculative-token argument D-165 made, applied to my own work. Components are deliberately out of scope. 34 have no consumer, but a design system legitimately ships ahead of its consumer and DataTable, Tabs and DatePicker are standard kit rather than fat; culling them is a different decision with a different rationale and should be made on its own.

designDecisions.question: The Alfons layout composition order — which layout wraps which — is recoverable from nothing: eight of nine layout components render no other layout, so the compose graph has one edge and sorting it produces a list that puts the outermost shell last. Where does the ordering live?
designDecisions.resolution: In an alfons.layout_tiers table beside alfons.lifecycle, joined into the manifest at build time. Four tiers, outermost first: shell (PageFrame, MainLayout, PageLayout), region (PageSection), container (Container, Grid, Stack, Inline, Center), primitive. The rule is that a component of a given tier may not contain one of an outer tier. get_layout_recipe and the layout-nesting rule both read this single source, so the recipe an agent is given and the rule it is judged against cannot disagree.
designDecisions.rationale: This is the same class of fact as lifecycle and it fails the same way, so it gets the same treatment under D-162. Composition order is a design judgement: nothing in a Stack says it belongs inside a PageFrame rather than around one, and the arrangement that is correct is correct because someone decided it. Deriving it anyway produced a confidently wrong answer — get_layout_recipe shipped in AL-004 ordering PageFrame last, and its tests passed because they checked the derivation was internally consistent rather than that the answer was right, which is the specific failure a derived-from-nothing field invites. A doc-comment field was the alternative and was rejected for the reason CLAUDE.md already records: an authored fact in a comment is how light mode, the focus ring and the fourth frost level were lost. Tiers rather than a total order because the real constraint is coarse — five container primitives are freely interchangeable and interchangeable in any order, and a total order would invent precedence between them that no one intends and that the rule would then enforce.

designDecisions.question: Thirty-six Alfons tokens form complete domain families — charting (--chart-*), confusion matrices (--matrix-*), A/B experiments (--experiment-*), heatmaps and seven --industry-*-gradient tokens — for surfaces that exist in no repository. Keep them against a future consumer, or remove them?
designDecisions.resolution: Retire and delete them. The definitions come out of colours.css and admin.css, and each name gets an alfons.lifecycle row citing this decision, so the manifest emits a tombstone. An agent reaching for --chart-tooltip-bg is told it was retired and why, rather than that it does not exist.
designDecisions.rationale: These are tokens designed against an imagined component rather than a built one, and the cost of keeping them is not storage — it is that they are indistinguishable from residue. The 110-orphan count is only actionable once every entry in it has an answer, and "speculative, for a chart layer nobody has written" is an answer that argues for removal: a token designed before its consumer encodes guesses about an API that does not exist, so the family that eventually ships will not match it anyway. AL-009's tombstones are what make deletion safe here in a way it was not for the AL-001 retirements — the judgement outlives the definition, which is precisely what light mode, the focus ring and the fourth frost level lacked when they were removed with only a CSS comment behind them.
